strengths: The unified multimodal flow formulation with decoupled (t, s) time axes is a clean and sensible extension of recent multimodal flow frameworks (Multiflow; Rojas et al.) to periodic crystal systems, and the paper convincingly demonstrates that a single trained model supports CSP, de novo generation, and atom-type generation without task-specific retraining (Figure 1, Algorithm 2).

The experimental evaluation is thorough and mostly convincing: CSP results are competitive with or superior to strong baselines (CrystalFlow, FlowMM, DiffCSP) on both MP-20 and the harder MPTS-52 benchmark (Table 1), and MCFlow notably reduces mode collapse toward low-symmetry space groups compared with FlowMM/ADiT (Figure 4), supporting the claim that the ordering/augmentation internalizes crystallographic symmetry.

The composition- and symmetry-aware atom ordering with hierarchical inter-/intra-orbit permutation augmentation is a concrete, well-motivated design choice, and its contribution is substantiated by cumulative ablations (Table 4) and a quantitative permutation-space reduction analysis (Appendix D, Figure 6).

Reproducibility support is strong: complete training/inference configurations (Tables 8-10), algorithms for training, inference, and noisy guidance (Algorithms 1-3), full metric definitions (Appendix G), guidance sensitivity/ablation studies (Appendix E), template-conditioned comparison (Table 11), scaling analysis across three model sizes (Figure 8), and stated compute resources.

The paper is honest about the template-conditioned setting being a different problem (excluded baselines with justifiable rationale) and provides an additional comparison under target-template filtering, and acknowledges limitations (scaling to larger unit cells) in the conclusion.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is largely incremental: the core machinery assembles known components (modality-wise decoupled time axes from Campbell et al. 2024 / Rojas et al. 2025, torus flow matching from FlowMM/Miller et al. 2024, DiT backbone, x1-prediction from Li & He 2025, Wyckoff-based ordering previously explored by Cao et al. 2024). The genuinely new elements are the electronegativity+Wyckoff lexicographic ordering and hierarchical permutation augmentation; the 'any-to-any' framing is also somewhat overstated since only two modalities (atom types, structures) are covered.

The ordering and augmentation rely on ground-truth symmetry analysis (space group / Wyckoff position detection, e.g., via spglib) of the training data, which introduces a dependency on symmetry-detection tolerances and robustness; the paper does not discuss sensitivity to orbit-detection errors, disordered/partially symmetric structures, or how the method behaves when detected symmetry is noisy.

No code release is mentioned anywhere in the manuscript, which weakens reproducibility despite the detailed configurations; several nontrivial components (orbit grouping, hierarchical permutation sampling, noisy guidance at the logit level) would be difficult to reimplement exactly.

The atom-type generation task (Section 4.3) is evaluated only against a deterministic CGCNN baseline with low absolute match rates (1-15%), and the significance of this task's evaluation is limited; a probabilistic conditional baseline would strengthen the comparison.

Symmetry distribution comparisons (Figure 4) are qualitative only, without a quantitative distributional metric (e.g., KL/Wasserstein over space groups), and no error bars or repeated-seed variance are reported for the main tables, making 'competitive' claims harder to assess precisely.

Baseline comparability is imperfect: several baseline numbers are taken from prior literature under potentially different data splits/protocols (the 60/20/20 split and MPTS-52 time-slice partition differ from common setups), and the paper does not state whether baselines were retrained under the identical protocol.

strengths: The unified formulation is well-motivated and cleanly executed: decoupling the flow time axes for atom types (CTMC) and structures (ODE) genuinely allows a single trained model to realize CSP, DNG, and structure-conditioned atom type generation via inference-time trajectory selection (Figure 1, Algorithms 2–3), avoiding task-specific retraining.

The composition- and symmetry-aware atom ordering with hierarchical inter-/intra-orbit permutation augmentation is a sensible way to inject crystallographic priors into a sequence-based DiT without structural templates, and the permutation-space analysis (Appendix D, Figure 6) quantifies the reduction (from ~10^18.4 to ~10^7.2 for N=20) rather than leaving it as a qualitative claim.

The evaluation is reasonably thorough for the claims made: two benchmarks (MP-20, MPTS-52), three model scales with consistent scaling behavior (Appendix H.3), component-wise ablations (Table 4), noisy-guidance ablation and sensitivity analysis (Table 7, Figure 7), and comparison under template-filtering against template-conditioned methods (Table 11).

The paper is honest about its positioning: it claims 'competitive' rather than superior performance, clearly separates full CSP from template-conditioned settings, and acknowledges in the conclusion that scaling to larger unit cells remains a challenge.

Reproducibility support is good at the documentation level: full training/inference hyperparameters (Tables 8–10), metric definitions (Appendix G), and algorithmic detail including the noisy-guidance inference procedure (Algorithm 3).
weaknesses: Originality is modest: the multimodal decoupled-time formulation is a direct adaptation of Campbell et al. (2024) and Rojas et al. (2025) to the crystalline domain, and the Wyckoff-based ordering builds on Cao et al. (2024). The domain-specific combination is competent but the conceptual novelty beyond prior multimodal flow and symmetry-ordering work is limited, and the paper does not isolate what is fundamentally new versus adapted.

Headline results are not clearly better than task-specific SOTA on the primary benchmark: on MP-20 CSP, CrystalFlow (20) achieves 78.34% MR versus at most 77.84% for MCFlow, and on DNG MCFlow-B trails ADiT on several metrics (e.g., d_ρ 0.136 vs 0.076, S.U.N. 15.1 vs 14.2 marginal). The unification gain over MPTS-52 is real but the MP-20 story is 'matching, not beating,' so the practical benefit of the unified framework rests mainly on convenience and symmetry-distribution fidelity (Figure 4).

A key inference ambiguity is not fully resolved: the ordering is defined via orbits under the space group and Wyckoff positions, but in CSP only the composition is observed at inference. The paper acknowledges this ambiguity in Section 3.2 but the main text does not specify concretely how conditioning atoms are ordered (and how ties among same-element atoms are broken) when structural symmetry information is unavailable; the mechanism appears to lean on permutation augmentation, which should be stated and validated explicitly.

No code release or supplementary artifact is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of a method whose ordering/augmentation details are intricate (orbit extraction, Wyckoff letter assignment, Niggli reduction, guidance implementation).

Results appear to come from single runs with no error bars or variance estimates across seeds; given that several headline comparisons (e.g., MCFlow-B vs CrystalFlow on MR, or MS.U.N. vs ADiT) are within a few points, statistical uncertainty is material and unreported.

The atom type generation task (Section 4.3) has only a weak deterministic baseline (CGCNN) with very low MR (3.50–4.71); the evaluation of this third task is comparatively shallow, and the claim of 'greater diversity' is supported mostly by qualitative samples.

Several baselines are excluded for the DNG comparison (FlowLLM, SymmCD, ADiT excluded from CSP; DiffCSP++/SGEquiDiff/SGFM excluded from full CSP), which is justified but still narrows the comparable field, and ADiT's inclusion of QM9 pretraining makes parts of Table 2 hard to interpret.

strengths: The unified any-to-any formulation is genuinely useful for the crystal generation community: a single trained model supports CSP, de novo generation, and atom type generation via trajectory selection in the (t,s) time plane, without task-specific retraining (Fig. 1, Alg. 2). The framing is clean and well-motivated.

The evaluation is thorough across three tasks on two benchmarks (MP-20, MPTS-52), with appropriate baselines and a defensible exclusion rationale for template-conditioned methods (Sec. 4.1). Results are genuinely competitive: e.g., MCFlow-L achieves 64.08% single-sample CSP MR on MP-20 and 27.16% on MPTS-52, and strong metastability (87.3% MS.U.N.) in DNG.

The observation that MCFlow better preserves space group / Wyckoff distributions relative to FlowMM and ADiT (Fig. 4) is an interesting and valuable empirical finding, supporting the claim that ordering + augmentation internalizes symmetry as a soft bias.

Ablations are well-designed: the cumulative ablation of inter-/intra-orbit permutation and positional embedding (Table 4), noisy guidance ablation (Table 7, Fig. 7), permutation space reduction analysis (Appendix D), scaling behavior across model sizes (Fig. 8), and template-conditioned comparison (Table 11) collectively support the component claims.

Reproducibility is strong: complete training/inference hyperparameters (Tables 8-10), full training and inference algorithms (Algs. 1-3), detailed flow-matching configurations per modality (Table 6), metric definitions (Appendix G), and compute costs are all provided.
The paper is clearly written, with a self-contained background appendix (flow matching on Euclidean, Riemannian, and discrete state spaces) that makes the method accessible.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty relative to prior work. The core machinery — decoupled modality-wise time axes for joint discrete-continuous flow — is directly adopted from Multiflow (Campbell et al., 2024) and Rojas et al. (2025), and noisy guidance is also borrowed from Rojas et al. The primary novelty is the application to periodic crystals plus the lexicographic electronegativity/Wyckoff ordering heuristic, which is an incremental extension of Cao et al. (2024)'s Wyckoff ordering.

A soundness ambiguity: the composition- and symmetry-aware ordering requires grouping atoms into orbits, which presupposes knowledge of the space group of the ground-truth (or generated) structure. The paper acknowledges that at CSP inference time structural symmetry is unavailable (Sec. 3.2), but the mechanism by which ordering is defined during iterative sampling (where the structure is only partially formed) is not clearly specified. Similarly, preprocessing relies on space group detection (e.g., pymatgen), an implicit use of symmetry information that slightly undercuts the 'without explicit symmetry constraints' framing.

The DiT backbone has no built-in SE(3)/periodic equivariance; permutation invariance is only encouraged through augmentation, and rotational/lattice equivariance is not addressed. This is a deliberate design choice but limits the inductive bias relative to equivariant competitors, and the paper does not analyze failure modes (e.g., how robustness degrades for low-symmetry P1 structures where the ordering provides little signal).

Headline CSP numbers are at parity rather than clearly superior: multi-sample MP-20 MR (77.84 for MCFlow-S) is essentially tied with DiffCSP (77.93) and only marginally above CrystalFlow (78.34 is higher). The MPTS-52 gains are the stronger result, but the claim of 'competitive or superior' should be read as parity on MP-20.

In DNG, uniqueness degrades substantially as model size increases (MS.U.N. drops from 41.4 to 16.8 from S to L), indicating mode concentration that the paper does not discuss or mitigate; this weakens the scaling story in Fig. 8.

Atom type generation results are weak in absolute terms (MR of 1-15% against a 4.71% deterministic baseline), and the significance of the match-rate metric in this setting is not well justified; the task reads more as a demonstration of framework flexibility than a useful capability.

Baseline comparability across datasets is uncertain: MPTS-52 uses a chronological time-slice split while MP-20 uses a random 60/20/20 split; it is unclear whether baseline numbers on MPTS-52 were reproduced under the same splits or taken from prior reports, which affects direct comparison.
No code release is mentioned, which limits practical reproducibility despite the thorough configuration details.

strengths: The unified multimodal flow formulation with decoupled time axes for atom types and structures is well motivated and cleanly instantiated; the resulting single model supports CSP, DNG, and structure-conditioned atom type generation without retraining, which is a genuine advance over task-specific crystal generative models.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: standard CSP metrics plus METRe/cRMSE polymorph-aware evaluation (Table H.2), filtered vs. unfiltered match rates (Table H.5), template-conditioned CSP (Table H.3), the standardized LeMat-GenBench DNG protocol with an MLIP ensemble (Table 2), and computational cost/saturation analyses (Table H.1, Figure 3).

Ablations are convincing: Table H.8 directly demonstrates that decoupled time axes are essential (MR drops from 63.14 to 45.58 with t=s and adapted DNG baselines collapse to 3.76/27.01), Table H.7 shows unified training matches CSP-only training, and Table 5/H.4 isolate contributions of electronegativity ordering, inter-/intra-orbit permutation, and positional embeddings.

The claim that the model internalizes crystallographic symmetry without explicit templates is supported by evidence beyond match rate: distribution matching over space groups and Wyckoff properties (Figure 4), and the qualitative atom-type substitution results (Table 4) aligning with known Materials Project entries.

Reproducibility is strong: complete architecture/training/inference configurations (Appendix F), full algorithms, resource requirements, wall-clock timings, public datasets, and standardized benchmark protocols.

Limitations are handled honestly (inapplicability to amorphous/disordered systems, stability-novelty trade-off with scale), and scaling behavior across three model sizes is reported rather than cherry-picking one size.
weaknesses: A key methodological detail is under-specified: the composition- and symmetry-aware ordering relies on orbits and Wyckoff positions computed from ground-truth structures during training/preprocessing, but during generation (especially DNG and CSP) neither the space group nor the structure is known a priori. The paper acknowledges ordering ambiguity for CSP but does not precisely explain how the ordering/PosEmb is determined while structures and atom types evolve during sampling. This matters because the ordering is claimed as a central contribution and its inference-time computation could either leak test-time symmetry information or require additional machinery.

Core conceptual novelty is moderate: the decoupled modality-time flow machinery is directly adopted from Multiflow (Campbell et al., 2024) and Rojas et al. (2025); the paper's distinct contributions are the adaptation to periodic systems and the ordering/augmentation heuristics. The writing could better delineate what is new versus inherited.

On MP-20 CSP the gains over the strongest baselines are marginal (single-sample MR: OMatG 63.75 vs. MCFlow-L 64.08), and noisy guidance yields only small improvements with no error bars or significance testing anywhere in the paper; several reported differences (e.g., MCFlow-B vs. MCFlow-L multi-sample MR, 77.12 vs. 76.08) could be within run-to-run variance.

Reported match-rate differences vs. baselines may partly reflect retraining on a 60/20/20 split rather than the original splits used by some baselines; cross-paper comparability of Table 1 numbers deserves more explicit discussion.

The ATG task comparison uses only two adapted baselines (CGCNN, FlowMM), so the ATG contribution, while interesting and apparently new as a stand-alone generative task, is less rigorously benchmarked than CSP/DNG.

Use of an autoregressive-free DiT with positional embeddings tied to a specific ordering means the inductive bias is only a soft one, and the paper's own limitation (failure on disordered structures) is a non-trivial restriction for a 'unified crystal modeling' claim; the impact on well-ordered but low-symmetry or partially occupied structures is not analyzed.

strengths: The unified formulation is well motivated and clearly articulated: decoupling flow time variables for atom types (discrete CTMC) and crystal structures (continuous ODE) allows CSP, DNG, and atom type generation to be realized as different inference trajectories in the (t,s) plane with a single trained model, and Table H.8 convincingly shows that coupled time axes (t=s) substantially degrade CSP performance.

The experimental evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: standardized CSP metrics with multiple recent baselines (CDVAE, DiffCSP, FlowMM, CrystalFlow, OMatG), the LeMat-GenBench protocol with an ensemble of three MLIPs for DNG, polymorph-aware METRe evaluation, filtered vs. unfiltered match rates, computational cost analysis (Table H.1), and scaling behavior across three model sizes.

The ablation studies are meaningful: Table 5 and H.4 isolate the contributions of electronegativity-based ordering vs. atomic number vs. random permutation, and the inter-/intra-orbit permutation augmentation; the ordering choice is empirically justified rather than assumed.

The paper provides strong evidence that a non-equivariant DiT with the proposed soft symmetry bias avoids the mode collapse toward P1 observed for FlowMM and ADiT (Figure 4), which is a genuine point in favor of the ordering approach over purely data-driven sequence models.

Reproducibility is good: full model/training/inference hyperparameters (Appendix F), algorithms for training and any-to-any inference with and without noisy guidance (Appendix C), metric definitions (Appendix G), and reasonable compute footprint (single RTX 3090/A40).
Limitations are honestly discussed: inapplicability to amorphous/disordered systems and a stability–novelty trade-off across scales.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is moderate: the any-to-any multimodal flow with decoupled time axes is directly borrowed from Multiflow (Campbell et al., 2024) and Rojas et al. (2025), the torus/geodesic treatment of fractional coordinates and LogNormal lattice priors follows FlowMM (Miller et al., 2024), and Wyckoff-based atom ordering was already proposed by Cao et al. (2025). The contribution is essentially a careful adaptation/combination of these ingredients to crystals plus an electronegativity-based ordering heuristic.

There is a potential circularity in the atom ordering that is not clearly resolved: the ordering and the hierarchical permutation augmentation require orbits, Wyckoff positions, and space-group information, yet for DNG (and during the CSP trajectory) the structure—and hence the symmetry labeling—is being generated and is not available a priori. The main text acknowledges this problem only for prior work's ordering, and does not precisely specify how orbits/Wyckoff labels are determined for intermediate generated states during inference. This ambiguity undermines the stated claim that the method works 'without explicit structural templates.'

Gains on the primary MP-20 benchmark are marginal: MCFlow-L (1) achieves 64.08 MR vs. OMatG's 63.75, and multi-sample MR (76.08–77.84) is at or below DiffCSP's 77.93. The stronger results are on MPTS-52, a less standard benchmark, so the headline claim of being 'competitive with task-specific baselines' rests heavily on one dataset.

The atom type generation (ATG) task, presented as a novel contribution, is compared only against adapted baselines (a deterministic CGCNN and an adapted FlowMM); the MR numbers for all methods are low (≤15.3%), and the practical value of the task is supported mostly by four qualitative substitution case studies (Table 4) rather than a systematic evaluation.

Stability of DNG outputs is assessed exclusively with MLIP surrogates (MACE-MP/UMA/Orb-v3); no DFT-level verification of any generated structures is provided, so claims of improved thermodynamic stability should be interpreted cautiously.

A stability–novelty trade-off is visible in Table 2: MCFlow-L has only 18.6% novelty with pre-relaxation, well below MatterGen (70.5%) and WyFormer (66.4%), and MSUN lags the small variant; the unified model does not clearly dominate on the composite discovery-oriented metrics.

Reliance on ground-truth space-group/Wyckoff annotations during preprocessing introduces a dependency on external symmetry-detection tooling (e.g., pymatgen's SpaceGroupAnalyzer) whose errors propagate into the ordering; the sensitivity of results to mislabeled or low-symmetry structures is not analyzed.

strengths: The paper delivers a genuinely useful unification: a single flow model supporting CSP, DNG, and structure-conditioned atom type generation via decoupled time axes, which prior crystal generators (DiffCSP, FlowMM, etc.) handle only in task-specific formulations. The claim that decoupled time axes matter is directly supported (Table H.8: coupled t=s drops MR from 63.14 to 45.58; adapted DNG baselines perform far worse), and unified training is shown not to hurt CSP performance (Table H.7).

Experimental evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: two benchmarks (MP-20, MPTS-52), a standardized third-party DNG protocol (LeMat-GenBench with an MLIP ensemble), polymorph-aware METRe/cRMSE evaluation, filtered vs. unfiltered match rates, computational cost comparisons (Table H.1), scaling behavior across three model sizes, and step-count saturation analysis (Figure 3).

The composition- and symmetry-aware atom ordering with hierarchical inter-/intra-orbit permutation augmentation is a well-motivated, novel inductive bias that lets a plain DiT learn crystallographic symmetry without explicit structural templates. It is carefully ablated (Tables 5, H.4), and the permutation-space reduction analysis (Appendix D) quantifies the design choice. The symmetry distribution analysis (Figure 4) showing avoidance of P1 mode collapse is a convincing qualitative demonstration.

Results are strong where it matters: best MPTS-52 CSP results across metrics, competitive MP-20 results, and leading DNG stability metrics (stability, metastability, E_hull) on LeMat-GenBench with and without pre-relaxation, at reasonable compute cost (Table H.1).

Limitations are discussed honestly and specifically (inapplicability to amorphous/disordered systems; stability-novelty trade-off with scale), and the any-to-any framing enables new capabilities such as atom type substitution with chemically meaningful top substitutions (Table 4).
Reproducibility is strong: complete hyperparameter tables, training/inference algorithms, base distribution fitting details, and hardware/training-time reporting are all provided.
weaknesses: Originality is moderate rather than high. The core machinery is an adaptation of existing components: decoupled multimodal time axes from Multiflow (Campbell et al., 2024) and Diffuse Everything (Rojas et al., 2025), a DiT backbone (Peebles & Xie, 2023), masked discrete flows for atom types, torus flow matching from FlowMM (Miller et al., 2024), and x1-prediction (Li & He, 2025). The genuinely new pieces are the electronegativity/Wyckoff ordering and hierarchical permutation augmentation, which are heuristically designed; the paper would benefit from deeper analysis of why this particular ordering works.

The ordering pipeline depends on ground-truth symmetry analysis (space group / Wyckoff position determination via pymatgen with a 0.1 Å tolerance) during preprocessing. No analysis is given of sensitivity to noisy or ambiguous symmetry assignments, and the method's reliance on well-defined symmetry is a real scope restriction (acknowledged, but underexplored).

On MP-20 CSP, gains over the strongest baselines are marginal (e.g., multi-sample MR 77.84/77.12 vs. DiffCSP's 77.93 and CrystalFlow's 78.34); the headline improvement is mainly on MPTS-52. Results appear to be single-seed; variance/significance across runs is not reported, so small margins (e.g., ablation deltas) are hard to assess statistically.

The novelty rate under pre-relaxation drops sharply with scale (70.5% for S down to 18.6% for L), revealing a stability-novelty trade-off that partially offsets the headline stability gains; this is acknowledged but not analyzed or mitigated.

The atom type substitution case study (Table 4) covers only four hand-picked materials with 100 samples each, and its validation (matching against known MP entries) is suggestive rather than a systematic evaluation.

The model is not permutation invariant by construction (fixed positional embeddings indexed by the proposed ordering), relying entirely on augmentation for symmetry robustness; a comparison against a genuinely invariant/equivariant conditioning alternative would strengthen the design justification.
No explicit code release statement appears in the manuscript, which limits reproducibility despite the detailed configuration reporting.
